name: creation
summary: Tensor construction, and the seeding of the default generator.
extended:
Thirty entry points: conversion (`tensor`, `as_tensor`, `from_numpy`), filled and `*_like` constructors, the range builders `arange` / `linspace`, the sampling family, the generator controls (`seed`, `get_rng_state` / `set_rng_state`, `initial_seed`, `randperm`) and DLPack exchange.

Every constructor takes `device=`, and passing it is what keeps a pipeline on one device: a helper built without it lands on the CPU and forces a round trip the moment it meets Metal data.

CPU and Metal share one default generator but consume it differently per draw — a CPU `rand(4)` advances its counter by 4, a Metal `rand(4)` by one block — so the same seed does not reproduce the same stream across devices; comparing them means comparing deterministic ops, replaying state with `get_rng_state()` / `set_rng_state()`, or `eval()` for anything stochastic.

returns.description: This generator, so a call can be chained.

methods.summary: The key this stream was last seeded with.

methods.name: seed
methods.summary: Reseed the stream from the OS entropy source and return the new key.

returns.description:
The key, in $[0, 2^{63})$; `manual_seed` with it
replays the stream from here.

members.summary: A Philox-4×32 random stream of its own.
members.extended:
Pass one as `generator=` to a random op to draw from it instead of the
default stream that `lucid.manual_seed` controls; draws through it
leave the default stream where it was.

parameters.name: seed
parameters.description:
The key, any integer in $[-2^{63}, 2^{64})$ — a negative one
is read modulo $2^{64}$, as the reference reads it.  When a
device specifier is given as the single positional argument
(`Generator("cpu")`), it is read as `device` and the key
defaults to `0`.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: The device recorded on `device`.  Defaults to `device("cpu")`.

raises.description: If `seed` is not an integer or device specifier.

If `seed` is out of the 64-bit range or `device` names no
supported device.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> g = lucid.Generator().manual_seed(7)
>>> g.initial_seed()
7
>>> a = lucid.rand(3, generator=g)
>>> state = g.get_state()
>>> b = lucid.rand(3, generator=g)
>>> c = lucid.rand(3, generator=g.set_state(state))
>>> bool((b == c).all())
True
notes:
The constructor accepts both `Generator(seed)` and the reference's
`Generator(device=...)` / `Generator("cpu")`.  `seed` reseeds
from entropy, as the reference's does; `initial_seed` reads the
key.

members.name: tensor
members.signature: tensor(data: object, dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False)
members.summary: Construct a new `Tensor` from Python data, a NumPy array, or another Tensor.
members.extended:
Always allocates a fresh storage and **copies** the source bytes into
Lucid-owned memory.  This is the canonical entry point for creating
tensors from heterogeneous Python inputs: scalars (`int` / `float` /
`bool`), nested lists, NumPy `ndarray`\s, and existing Lucid
`Tensor`\s.  Dtype is inferred from the source unless `dtype` is
given; device defaults to the global default (typically `"cpu"`) unless
overridden.

parameters.name: data
parameters.description:
Source data.  Accepted forms:

* Python scalar (`bool`, `int`, `float`, `complex`) or
  NumPy scalar — produces a 0-d tensor.
* Nested `list` / `tuple` of those — recursively converted;
  the nesting must be rectangular.
* `numpy.ndarray` — bridge boundary
  (see `lucid._factories.converters`); the data is copied
  regardless of the source array's contiguity.
* Existing `Tensor` — copied to a new buffer and detached
  from its autograd graph, so the result is a leaf of its own (use
  `as_tensor` to avoid the copy when dtype/device match).

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description:
Target element type.  `None` (default) infers from `data`:
`bool` → `bool`, `int` → `int64`, `float` → the default
dtype (`get_default_dtype`), `complex` → its complex counterpart
(`complex128` under a `float64` default, else `complex64`);
a NumPy scalar or array, or a Tensor, keeps its own dtype.  Mixed
elements take the highest kind (bool < int < float < complex) at
the widest width among them.  Integers are stored exactly at any
magnitude; a value the dtype cannot hold raises — `TypeError`
for a complex into a real dtype, `ValueError` for NaN or
infinity into an integer dtype, `OverflowError` for an integer
out of range.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description:
Target device (`"cpu"` or `"metal"`).  `None` uses
`lucid.get_default_device`, except that a Tensor stays on its
own device.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description:
Whether the resulting tensor should record autograd operations.
The result is always a leaf, whatever the dtype conversion.
Defaults to `False`.

returns.description: A freshly-allocated Lucid tensor.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
tensor([1., 2., 3.])
>>> lucid.tensor([[1, 2], [3, 4]], dtype=lucid.float32)
tensor([[1., 2.],
        [3., 4.]])
>>> import numpy as np
>>> lucid.tensor(np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3))
tensor([[0, 1, 2],
        [3, 4, 5]], dtype=lucid.int64)
>>> src = lucid.tensor([1.0, 2.0], requires_grad=True)
>>> copy = lucid.tensor(src, dtype=lucid.float64)
>>> copy.dtype, copy.is_leaf, copy.requires_grad
(lucid.float64, True, False)
notes:
This factory is one of the six "bridge" entry points in the **H4** rule
— the only places where external libraries (NumPy here) may legitimately
cross into Lucid's compute path.  Outside the bridges, Lucid composites
must use engine primitives directly.

For zero-copy conversion when the source is already an `ndarray` on
CPU and shares dtype, prefer `as_tensor`.

members.name: as_tensor
members.signature: as_tensor(data: object, dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None)
members.summary: Convert data to a tensor, avoiding a copy when the source already matches.
members.extended:
Unlike `tensor`, `as_tensor` is "best-effort no-copy":

* If `data` is already a `Tensor` with the requested `dtype`
  and `device`, it is returned unchanged.
* If `data` is a `Tensor` whose dtype or device differs, it is
  converted as `Tensor.to` converts it, and the result stays
  connected to `data`'s autograd graph — unlike `tensor`, which
  copies into a detached leaf.
* Anything else — Python data, NumPy arrays — goes through
  `tensor`, which copies.

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: Source data — Python scalar / list, NumPy array, or Tensor.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description: Target element type.  `None` preserves the source dtype.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description:
Target device.  When the source already lives on a different device,
a copy across the device boundary is performed.

returns.description:
`data` itself, a converted copy of it, or a freshly-constructed
Lucid tensor.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> x = lucid.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
>>> lucid.as_tensor(x) is x              # already a Tensor, returned as-is
True
>>> lucid.as_tensor(x, dtype=lucid.float64).dtype
lucid.float64
>>> w = lucid.tensor([1.0, 2.0], requires_grad=True)
>>> lucid.as_tensor(w, dtype=lucid.float64).sum().backward()
>>> w.grad                               # the conversion stays in the graph
tensor([1., 1.])
notes:
`as_tensor` is the right choice in code that may be handed either a
Tensor or raw data (e.g. a collate function): a Tensor that already has
the requested dtype and device passes through with no allocation at
all.  For semantic clarity in library code that should never share
storage, use `tensor`.

members.name: from_numpy
members.signature: from_numpy(ndarray: np.ndarray)
members.summary: Copy a NumPy `ndarray` into an owned Lucid tensor.
members.extended:
The returned tensor owns a copy and inherits the array's dtype according
to the canonical
NumPy → Lucid mapping (`np.float32` → `lucid.float32`,
`np.int64` → `lucid.int64`, etc.). Mutations do not propagate between
the source array and the result. Like `tensor`, this bridge uses
the active default device; use `tensor(arr, device="cpu")` to pin it.

parameters.name: ndarray
parameters.description:
Source array.  Must reside in CPU memory.  Any layout (C / Fortran /
strided) is accepted and copied to contiguous owned storage.

returns.description: A tensor with copied values on the active default device.

raises.description:
If the array dtype has no corresponding Lucid dtype. The native
`DtypeMismatch` exception derives from `RuntimeError`; object
arrays, for example, are rejected.
If a `uint64` array holds a value past `int64`'s range.

examples:
>>> import lucid, numpy as np
>>> arr = np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]], dtype=np.float32)
>>> t = lucid.from_numpy(arr)
>>> t.dtype
lucid.float32
>>> arr[0, 0] = 99.0          # mutate the source
>>> t[0, 0].item()            # the owned copy is unchanged
1.0
notes:
Lucid has no unsigned integer dtypes, so unsigned arrays widen
losslessly to the next signed width: `uint8` to `int16`, `uint16`
to `int32`, `uint32` and `uint64` to `int64`.

This is one of the documented **H4** bridge boundaries — the only places
where Lucid is allowed to take a NumPy array as input.  To move the
result onto a Metal device, chain `Tensor.to`:

    t = lucid.from_numpy(arr).to("metal")

members.name: from_dlpack
members.signature: from_dlpack(ext_tensor: object, device: DeviceLike = None, copy: _bool | None = None)
members.summary:
Construct a Lucid tensor from any object exposing the DLPack
protocol (`__dlpack__`) or from a raw PyCapsule.
members.extended:
Two dialects, picked by what the producer says it is:

* **Metal** (`__dlpack_device__() == (8, 0)`) — adopted natively.
  The producer's `MTLBuffer` becomes this tensor's storage with no
  copy at all, which is what makes an `mlx.core.array` and a Lucid
  Metal tensor two views of one allocation. NumPy cannot read a
  capsule of this device type, so this path bypasses it entirely.
* **Everything else** — through NumPy, which shares host memory
  where it can. The result lives on the CPU by default unless
  `device` is explicitly specified.

Requires numpy for the host dialect — install via
`pip install lucid[numpy]` if missing. The Metal dialect needs
nothing.

parameters.name: ext_tensor
parameters.description: An object exposing `__dlpack__` or a raw DLPack `PyCapsule`.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Target device for the returned tensor.

parameters.name: copy
parameters.description:
If `True`, always copy the data; if `False`, raise `BufferError`
when a copy is required.

members.name: to_dlpack
members.signature: to_dlpack(tensor: Tensor)
members.summary: Export `tensor` as a DLPack PyCapsule.
members.extended:
A Metal tensor exports natively — the capsule carries its
`MTLBuffer`, so an MLX consumer reads the same pages rather than a
downloaded copy. A CPU tensor materialises through NumPy. Either
capsule can be consumed exactly once.

Requires numpy for the host dialect — install via
`pip install lucid[numpy]` if missing.

members.name: zeros
members.signature: zeros(size: _int | tuple[_int, ...] = (), dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False)
members.summary: Return a tensor filled with the additive identity element, zero.
members.extended:
Allocates a new tensor of the requested shape and fills every element
with the scalar value $0$.  The result is the unique tensor satisfying

$$
Z_{i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_n} = 0
\quad \forall\; (i_1, \ldots, i_n) \in \prod_k [0, s_k)
$$

where $(s_1, \ldots, s_n)$ is the requested shape.

Zero-initialisation is the standard starting point for accumulation
buffers (gradient accumulators, running statistics in batch norm,
confusion matrices) and for masking computations where a neutral
additive element is required.

parameters.name: *size
parameters.description:
Shape of the output tensor.  Can be passed as separate positional
integers `zeros(2, 3)` or as a single tuple `zeros((2, 3))`.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description:
Scalar data type of the output.  Defaults to the global default
dtype (`lucid.float32` unless changed with
`lucid.set_default_dtype`).

parameters.name: device
parameters.description:
Target device — `"cpu"` (Apple Accelerate) or `"metal"`
(Apple Metal GPU).  Defaults to the global default device.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description:
If `True`, operations on the returned tensor are recorded by the
autograd engine.  Default: `False`.

returns.description: Tensor of shape `size` filled with zeros.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.zeros(3).tolist()
[0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
>>> lucid.zeros(2, 3).shape
(2, 3)
>>> lucid.zeros((4,), dtype=lucid.int32).dtype
lucid.int32
Accumulate squared errors manually:
>>> acc = lucid.zeros(1)
>>> for x in [1.0, -2.0, 3.0]:
...     acc = acc + lucid.tensor(x) ** 2
notes:
On Metal, the allocation and fill are performed on-device without a
host round-trip.  Gradient of `zeros` with respect to any upstream
variable is always zero by linearity, so it is never placed on the
computation graph as a leaf that affects gradients — but downstream
operations on it *are* tracked when `requires_grad=True`.

members.name: ones
members.signature: ones(size: _int | tuple[_int, ...] = (), dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False)
members.summary: Return a tensor filled with the multiplicative identity element, one.
members.extended:
Allocates a new tensor of the requested shape and fills every element
with the scalar value $1$.  Every entry satisfies

$$
O_{i_1, \ldots, i_n} = 1
\quad \forall\; (i_1, \ldots, i_n) \in \prod_k [0, s_k)
$$

One-initialisation is the canonical starting point for multiplicative
accumulators, scale parameters in normalisation layers (before any
training), and homogeneous coordinate vectors in projective geometry.

parameters.name: *size
parameters.description:
Shape of the output tensor.  Accepts separate ints
`ones(2, 3)` or a single tuple `ones((2, 3))`.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description:
Scalar data type.  Defaults to the global default dtype
(`lucid.float32` unless overridden).

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Target device — `"cpu"` or `"metal"`.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description:
If `True`, downstream operations are tracked by autograd.
Default: `False`.

returns.description: Tensor of shape `size` filled with ones.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.ones(4).tolist()
[1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
>>> lucid.ones(2, 2, dtype=lucid.int8)
tensor([[1, 1],
        [1, 1]], dtype=lucid.int8)
Row-sum via matrix-vector product:
>>> A = lucid.tensor([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]])
>>> row_sums = A @ lucid.ones(2)
>>> row_sums.tolist()
[3.0, 7.0]
notes:
The all-ones vector $\mathbf{1} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ plays an important
role in matrix algebra: multiplying a matrix $A$ on the right by
$\mathbf{1}$ computes its row sums, $A\mathbf{1} = \text{rowsum}(A)$.
This is useful when implementing attention masks, normalisation
denominators, and indicator functions.

members.name: empty
members.signature: empty(size: _int | tuple[_int, ...] = (), dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False)
members.summary: Return a tensor whose elements are uninitialised (undefined memory).
members.extended:
Allocates the backing memory for the requested shape but performs **no
initialisation write**.  Reading any element before overwriting it is
undefined behaviour — values may be zero, garbage, or a previous
tensor's data depending on the allocator's state.

The key advantage over `zeros` or `ones` is that the initialisation
kernel is skipped entirely, which is measurable when allocating large
temporary buffers inside hot loops.  The typical pattern is:

$$
\text{allocate} \to \text{fill via in-place op} \to \text{read}
$$

parameters.name: *size
parameters.description:
Shape of the output tensor.  Accepts separate ints
`empty(2, 3)` or a single tuple `empty((2, 3))`.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description: Scalar data type.  Defaults to the global default dtype.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Target device — `"cpu"` or `"metal"`.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description:
If `True`, downstream operations are tracked by autograd.
Default: `False`.

returns.description: Uninitialised tensor of shape `size`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> t = lucid.empty(3, 4)
>>> t.shape
(3, 4)
Safe usage — always overwrite before reading:
>>> buf = lucid.empty(5)
>>> buf[:] = lucid.arange(5.0)
>>> buf.tolist()
[0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]
notes:
Never use `empty` as input to a computation that reads its values
without first writing them.  Common safe patterns:

- `out = lucid.empty(n); lucid.matmul(a, b, out=out)`
- Passing as a pre-allocated output buffer to in-place operations

On Metal the memory is allocated in the device heap; the allocator
may reuse pages from recently freed tensors, so values are truly
unpredictable.

members.name: empty_strided
members.signature: empty_strided(size: Sequence[_int], stride: Sequence[_int], dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False)
members.summary: Create an uninitialised tensor with the specified `size` and `stride`.

parameters.name: size
parameters.description: Shape of the output tensor.

parameters.name: stride
parameters.description: Stride of the output tensor (in elements).

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description: Scalar data type. Defaults to the global default dtype.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Target device — `"cpu"` or `"metal"`.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description: If `True`, downstream operations are tracked by autograd.

returns.description: Uninitialised tensor with shape `size` and stride `stride`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> t = lucid.empty_strided((2, 3), (3, 1))
>>> (t.shape, t.stride())
((2, 3), (3, 1))

members.name: full
members.signature: full(size: _int | list[_int] | tuple[_int, ...], fill_value: _complex, dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False)
members.summary: Return a tensor filled with a constant scalar value.
members.extended:
Every element of the output equals `fill_value`:

$$
F_{i_1, \ldots, i_n} = c
\quad \forall\; (i_1, \ldots, i_n) \in \prod_k [0, s_k)
$$

where $c$ is `fill_value`.  This is a generalisation of `zeros`
($c = 0$) and `ones` ($c = 1$) to an arbitrary constant.

parameters.name: size
parameters.description:
Shape of the output tensor.  Unlike the `*size` varargs of
`zeros` / `ones`, this is a single positional argument, so
multi-dimensional shapes must be passed as a list or tuple:
`full((2, 3), 7.0)`.

parameters.name: fill_value
parameters.description:
The scalar constant to broadcast across all elements.  It is
stored exactly in `dtype`: an integer keeps every digit (the
fill does not pass through a double) and a complex keeps its
imaginary part.  A complex value into a real `dtype` raises
`TypeError`, a non-finite float into an integer `dtype`
`ValueError`, and an integer outside `dtype`'s range
`OverflowError`.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description:
Scalar data type.  If `None`, inferred from `fill_value`
(integers → `int64`, floats → the global default float dtype).

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Target device — `"cpu"` or `"metal"`.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description:
If `True`, downstream operations are tracked by autograd.
Default: `False`.

returns.description: Constant tensor of shape `size` filled with `fill_value`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.full((2, 3), 3.14).shape
(2, 3)
>>> lucid.full(4, -1.0).tolist()
[-1.0, -1.0, -1.0, -1.0]
Mask of a fixed value (e.g. $-\infty$ for attention masking):
>>> mask = lucid.full((4, 4), float("-inf"))
Integers past $2^{53}$ and complex values are stored exactly:
>>> lucid.full((1,), 2**60 + 1, dtype=lucid.int64).item()
1152921504606846977
>>> lucid.full((2,), 2 + 3j, dtype=lucid.complex64).tolist()
[(2+3j), (2+3j)]
notes:
Every output element is assigned `fill_value` exactly — there is no
broadcasting needed once the scalar reaches the engine.  When
`dtype` is omitted, the type is inferred from the Python type of
`fill_value`: `int` literals promote to `int64` and `float`
literals to the global default floating dtype (`lucid.float32` by
default).  If `fill_value` is a 0-d tensor (`Tensor` of shape
`()`), its scalar value is extracted via `Tensor.item` and
broadcast across the full tensor; element-wise broadcasting from a
larger tensor is not supported here (use `lucid.broadcast_to`
instead).

members.name: eye
members.signature: eye(n: _int, m: _int | None = None, dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False)
members.summary: Return a 2-D matrix with ones on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere.
members.extended:
The returned matrix $E \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}$ is defined by the
Kronecker delta:

$$
E_{ij} = \delta_{ij} =
\begin{cases}
    1 & \text{if } i = j \\
    0 & \text{if } i \neq j
\end{cases}
$$

When $n = m$ this is the identity matrix $I_n$, which satisfies
$I_n A = A I_n = A$ for any $n \times n$ matrix $A$.  Rectangular
variants ($n \neq m$) arise naturally as the pseudo-identity in
least-squares problems and in constructing projection matrices.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Number of rows.

parameters.name: m
parameters.description: Number of columns.  Defaults to `n`, yielding a square identity.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description:
Scalar data type.  Defaults to the global default dtype
(`lucid.float32` unless overridden).

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Target device — `"cpu"` or `"metal"`.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description:
If `True`, downstream operations are tracked by autograd.
Default: `False`.

returns.description: 2-D tensor of shape `(n, m)` with $E_{ij} = \delta_{ij}$.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.eye(3)
tensor([[1., 0., 0.],
        [0., 1., 0.],
        [0., 0., 1.]])
Rectangular variant:
>>> lucid.eye(2, 4)
tensor([[1., 0., 0., 0.],
        [0., 1., 0., 0.]])
Verify $I A = A$:
>>> A = lucid.tensor([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
>>> (lucid.eye(2) @ A - A).abs().max()
tensor(0.)
notes:
The identity matrix is its own inverse and its own transpose:
$I_n^{-1} = I_n^\top = I_n$.  Its eigenvalues are all $1$, and it
is simultaneously orthogonal, symmetric, idempotent ($I^2 = I$),
and unitary.

In deep learning, identity initialisations are used in recurrent
networks (e.g. the IRNN, Le et al. 2015) to preserve gradient norms
across time steps, exploiting the fact that the spectral radius of
$I$ is exactly $1$.

members.name: arange
members.signature: arange(start: _float, end: _float | None = None, step: _float = 1, dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False)
members.summary: Return a 1-D tensor of evenly spaced values over a half-open interval.
members.extended:
Generates the arithmetic sequence

$$
x_k = \texttt{start} + k \cdot \texttt{step},
\quad k = 0, 1, \ldots, N-1
$$

where $N = \left\lceil \dfrac{\texttt{end} - \texttt{start}}{\texttt{step}} \right\rceil$
is the number of elements.  The interval is **half-open**: `start`
is included, `end` is excluded, mirroring Python's built-in
`range`.

When called with a single positional argument `arange(n)`, the call
is reinterpreted as `arange(0, n, 1)`, yielding
$[0, 1, \ldots, n-1]$.

parameters.name: start
parameters.description:
Starting value of the sequence (inclusive).  When `end` is
`None`, this argument is treated as `end` and `start` is
set to `0`.

parameters.name: end
parameters.description:
End of the interval (exclusive).  Required unless using the
single-argument form.

parameters.name: step
parameters.description:
Spacing between consecutive values.  May be negative (producing
a decreasing sequence) provided `start > end`.  Default: `1`.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description:
Scalar data type of the output.  If `None`, inferred from
`start`, `end` and `step`: when every one of them is an
integer the result is `int64`, and a single float among them
makes it the global default float dtype (`get_default_dtype`).
A `bool`, another library's integer scalar and a
single-element integer tensor all count as integers.  An explicit
`dtype` always wins.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Target device — `"cpu"` or `"metal"`.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description:
If `True`, the sequence comes back as a leaf whose operations
autograd records.  Default: `False`.

returns.description: 1-D tensor containing the arithmetic sequence.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> x = lucid.arange(5)
>>> x.tolist(), x.dtype
([0, 1, 2, 3, 4], lucid.int64)
One float argument makes the result floating point:
>>> y = lucid.arange(1.0, 2.0, 0.25)
>>> y.tolist(), y.dtype
([1.0, 1.25, 1.5, 1.75], lucid.float32)
Descending sequence:
>>> lucid.arange(5, 0, -1).tolist()
[5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
An explicit dtype overrides the rule, as for position encoding
indices that are wanted as floats:
>>> lucid.arange(4, dtype=lucid.float32).tolist()
[0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
Integers past $2^{53}$ stay exact:
>>> lucid.arange(2**53 + 1, 2**53 + 3).tolist()
[9007199254740993, 9007199254740994]
notes:
Due to floating-point rounding, the number of elements may differ
from the naively expected $\lceil (\texttt{end} - \texttt{start}) /
\texttt{step} \rceil$ by $\pm 1$.  When exact element counts matter,
prefer `linspace` which always produces exactly `steps` values.

The last element is always **strictly less than** `end` (for
positive `step`) or **strictly greater than** `end` (for negative
`step`).

An `int64` result is exact at any magnitude.  The engine computes
each element in double precision, which holds integers exactly only
up to $2^{53}$, so a range reaching past that is built from Python
integers instead.

members.name: linspace
members.signature: linspace(start: _float, end: _float, steps: _int, dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False)
members.summary: Return a 1-D tensor of `steps` equally spaced values over a closed interval.
members.extended:
Generates the arithmetic sequence

$$
x_k = \texttt{start} + k \cdot \frac{\texttt{end} - \texttt{start}}{\texttt{steps} - 1},
\quad k = 0, 1, \ldots, \texttt{steps} - 1
$$

Unlike `arange`, the interval is **closed** on both ends: `start`
and `end` are both included in the output, and the number of
elements is always exactly `steps`.

parameters.name: start
parameters.description: Starting value of the sequence (inclusive).

parameters.name: end
parameters.description: Ending value of the sequence (inclusive).

parameters.name: steps
parameters.description:
Number of evenly spaced samples.  Must be $\geq 1$.
When `steps = 1` the output contains only `start`.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description: Scalar data type.  Defaults to the global default float dtype.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Target device — `"cpu"` or `"metal"`.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description:
If `True`, the samples form a leaf tensor that autograd tracks.
Default: `False`.

returns.description: 1-D tensor of shape `(steps,)` with evenly spaced values.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 5).tolist()
[0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0]
Sinusoidal position encoding grid:
>>> t = lucid.linspace(0.0, 2 * 3.14159, 64)
>>> t.shape
(64,)
Single-element edge case:
>>> lucid.linspace(3.0, 7.0, 1).tolist()
[3.0]
notes:
`linspace` is preferable to `arange` whenever:

* The exact number of points is prescribed (e.g. FFT grid,
  sinusoidal position encodings, Gaussian quadrature nodes).
* Floating-point rounding in the step size would cause off-by-one
  element counts.

The spacing between consecutive elements is exactly
$\Delta = (\texttt{end} - \texttt{start}) / (\texttt{steps} - 1)$,
so the output satisfies $x_{\texttt{steps}-1} = \texttt{end}$ to
within floating-point precision.

For frequency grids in signal processing the common pattern is:



$$
f_k = \frac{k}{N} \cdot f_s, \quad k = 0, \ldots, N-1
$$

which can be constructed as `linspace(0, fs, N, endpoint=False)`
(use `arange(N) / N * fs` for the half-open variant).

members.name: zeros_like
members.signature: zeros_like(input: Tensor, dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False)
members.summary: Return a zero-filled tensor with the same shape, dtype, and device as `input`.
members.extended:
Equivalent to `lucid.zeros(t.shape, dtype=t.dtype, device=t.device)`,
but infers the metadata from an existing tensor so the caller need not
repeat it.  Every element satisfies

$$
Z_{i_1, \ldots, i_n} = 0
\quad \forall\; (i_1, \ldots, i_n) \in \prod_k [0, s_k)
$$

where $(s_1, \ldots, s_n) = \texttt{t.shape}$.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description:
Reference tensor.  Its `shape`, `dtype`, and `device` are
used as defaults for the output.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description:
Override the data type.  When `None` (default), inherits
`t.dtype`.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description:
Override the device.  When `None` (default), inherits
`t.device`.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description:
If `True`, downstream operations are tracked by autograd.
Default: `False`.

returns.description: Zero tensor with the same shape (and optionally dtype/device) as `input`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> w = lucid.randn(3, 4, dtype=lucid.float16, device="metal")
>>> g = lucid.zeros_like(w)
>>> g.shape, g.dtype, g.device
((3, 4), lucid.float16, device('metal'))
Override dtype on-the-fly:
>>> mask = lucid.zeros_like(w, dtype=lucid.bool_)
notes:
A common use case is zeroing out a gradient accumulator that has the
same shape as a parameter tensor:



$$
g \leftarrow \mathbf{0}_{\text{like}(\theta)}
$$

This avoids hard-coding shape constants and ensures dtype consistency
(e.g. `float16` parameters get `float16` zero gradients).

members.name: ones_like
members.signature: ones_like(input: Tensor, dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False)
members.summary: Return an all-ones tensor with the same shape, dtype, and device as `input`.
members.extended:
Equivalent to `lucid.ones(t.shape, dtype=t.dtype, device=t.device)`,
but infers metadata from an existing tensor.  Every element satisfies

$$
O_{i_1, \ldots, i_n} = 1
\quad \forall\; (i_1, \ldots, i_n) \in \prod_k [0, s_k)
$$

parameters.name: input
parameters.description:
Reference tensor whose `shape`, `dtype`, and `device` are
used as defaults.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description: Override the data type.  Defaults to `t.dtype`.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Override the device.  Defaults to `t.device`.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description: Enable autograd tracking on the output.  Default: `False`.

returns.description: All-ones tensor shaped like `input`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> x = lucid.randn(2, 8)
>>> gamma = lucid.ones_like(x)
>>> gamma.shape
(2, 8)
Initialise scale parameters of a normalisation layer:
>>> weight = lucid.ones_like(x, requires_grad=True)
notes:
Multiplicative identity initialisation is used in layer-normalisation
and group-normalisation to set the learnable scale parameter $\gamma$
to $1$ at the start of training, so the network begins as a pure
normalisation with no learned rescaling:



$$
\hat{x} = \gamma \cdot \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} + \beta,
\quad \gamma_0 = \mathbf{1},\; \beta_0 = \mathbf{0}
$$

members.name: empty_like
members.signature: empty_like(input: Tensor, dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False)
members.summary: Return an uninitialised tensor with the same shape, dtype, and device as `input`.
members.extended:
Allocates backing memory matching `input`'s metadata but performs no
initialisation write.  Reading elements before overwriting them is
undefined behaviour.  The typical use is to pre-allocate an output
buffer for an in-place kernel call:

$$
\text{allocate}(|\texttt{t}|) \;\to\; \text{kernel\_write}(\text{buf})
\;\to\; \text{read}(\text{buf})
$$

parameters.name: input
parameters.description:
Reference tensor whose `shape`, `dtype`, and `device` are
inherited by the output.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description: Override the data type.  Defaults to `t.dtype`.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Override the device.  Defaults to `t.device`.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description: Enable autograd tracking.  Default: `False`.

returns.description: Uninitialised tensor shaped like `input`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> x = lucid.randn(1024, 1024)
>>> buf = lucid.empty_like(x)     # fast scratch space
>>> buf.shape
(1024, 1024)
notes:
Skipping the zero-fill write is only a win when the allocation is
large and will be fully overwritten before any read.  For small
tensors the branch-prediction and cache effects of the explicit
initialisation kernel are negligible; prefer `zeros_like` in those
cases for safety.

members.name: full_like
members.signature: full_like(input: Tensor, fill_value: _complex, dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False)
members.summary: Return a constant-filled tensor with the same shape, dtype, and device as `input`.
members.extended:
Every element of the output equals `fill_value`:

$$
F_{i_1, \ldots, i_n} = c
\quad \forall\; (i_1, \ldots, i_n) \in \prod_k [0, s_k)
$$

where $c = \texttt{fill\_value}$ and $(s_1, \ldots, s_n) = \texttt{t.shape}$.
This is the shape-aware generalisation of `full`.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description:
Reference tensor.  Shape, dtype, and device are inherited unless
overridden by the keyword arguments.

parameters.name: fill_value
parameters.description:
Scalar constant to broadcast across all elements, stored exactly
in the result's dtype as `full` stores it.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description:
Override the data type.  The value is filled in this dtype
directly, not filled in `t.dtype` and cast — so
`full_like(int_tensor, 2.5, dtype=lucid.float32)` holds `2.5`.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Override the device.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description:
If `True`, the constant tensor is a leaf recorded by autograd.
Default: `False`.

returns.description: Constant tensor shaped like `input`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> scores = lucid.randn(4, 8)
>>> mask = lucid.full_like(scores, float("-inf"))
>>> mask.shape
(4, 8)
Constant padding value:
>>> x = lucid.randn(2, 3)
>>> padded = lucid.full_like(x, -1.0)
notes:
A canonical application is initialising the **attention bias mask**
before selectively unmasking positions.  Starting from
$-\infty$ on a tensor shaped like the attention weight matrix ensures
that masked positions become zero after softmax:



$$
\text{logit}_{ij} \leftarrow
\begin{cases}
  \text{logit}_{ij} & \text{unmasked} \\
  -\infty           & \text{masked}
\end{cases}
\implies
\text{softmax}(\text{logit})_i \;=\; 0 \text{ for masked } j
$$

members.name: logspace
members.signature: logspace(start: _float, end: _float, steps: _int, base: _float = 10.0, dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False)
members.summary: Return a 1-D tensor of `steps` values evenly spaced on a logarithmic scale.
members.extended:
Generates the geometric sequence

$$
x_k = \texttt{base}^{y_k},
\quad y_k = \texttt{start} + k \cdot \frac{\texttt{end} - \texttt{start}}{\texttt{steps} - 1},
\quad k = 0, 1, \ldots, \texttt{steps} - 1
$$

Equivalently, the exponents $y_k$ are linearly spaced (as in
`linspace`) and then the base is raised to those exponents.  The
result spans the range $[\texttt{base}^\texttt{start},\,
\texttt{base}^\texttt{end}]$ multiplicatively: consecutive elements
satisfy $x_{k+1} / x_k = \text{const}$.

parameters.name: start
parameters.description:
Exponent of the first value.  The first element equals
$\texttt{base}^\texttt{start}$.

parameters.name: end
parameters.description:
Exponent of the last value.  The last element equals
$\texttt{base}^\texttt{end}$.

parameters.name: steps
parameters.description: Number of samples.  Must be $\geq 1$.

parameters.name: base
parameters.description:
Logarithm base.  Common choices:

* `10.0` (default) — decades, used in frequency / magnitude plots
* `2.0` — octaves, used in learning-rate schedules and wavelets
* `math.e` ($\approx 2.718$) — natural exponential spacing

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description: Scalar data type.  Defaults to the global default float dtype.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Target device — `"cpu"` or `"metal"`.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description:
If `True`, a loss built from the result fills its `.grad` on
`backward()` — it is returned as a leaf.  Default: `False`.

returns.description: 1-D tensor of shape `(steps,)` with geometrically spaced values.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.logspace(0, 3, 4).tolist()
[1.0, 10.0, 100.0, 1000.0]
Two-octave learning-rate sweep (base 2):
>>> lrs = lucid.logspace(-8, -1, 8, base=2.0)
>>> lrs.tolist()
[0.00390625, 0.0078125, ..., 0.5]
Sinusoidal position encoding frequencies (Transformer convention):
>>> d_model = 512
>>> inv_freq = lucid.logspace(0, -1, d_model // 2, base=10000.0)
notes:
Logarithmic spacing appears in:

* **Learning-rate grid search** — scanning
  $[10^{-5}, 10^{-1}]$ with `logspace(-5, -1, 9)` covers five
  decades uniformly in log-space rather than concentrating samples
  near the upper bound as linear spacing would.
* **Frequency analysis** — the mel and bark scales approximate
  human auditory perception and are nearly logarithmic in Hz.
* **Sinusoidal position encodings** (Vaswani et al., 2017) use
  $\omega_k = 10000^{-2k/d}$, which is a logspace on base $10000$.

The ratio between adjacent elements is constant:



$$
\frac{x_{k+1}}{x_k}
= \texttt{base}^{\,(\texttt{end}-\texttt{start})\,/\,(\texttt{steps}-1)}
$$

members.name: manual_seed
members.signature: manual_seed(seed: _int)
members.summary: Set the key to `seed` and rewind the stream to its start.

parameters.name: seed
parameters.description: The new key, as for the constructor.

returns.description: This generator, so a call can be chained.

members.name: seed
members.signature: seed()
members.summary: Reseed the stream from the OS entropy source and return the new key.

returns.description:
The key, in $[0, 2^{63})$; `manual_seed` with it
replays the stream from here.

members.name: initial_seed
members.signature: initial_seed()
members.summary: The key this stream was last seeded with.

members.name: get_rng_state
members.signature: get_rng_state()
members.summary: Snapshot the full state of the default random generator.
members.extended:
Returns an `int64` tensor of length 2, `[seed, counter]`,
that completely characterises the default Philox generator.

The Philox-4×32 PRNG is a **stateless counter-based** design: the
entire infinite sample stream is determined by the two-tuple

$$
\text{state} = (k,\; c)
\quad k \in [0,\, 2^{63}),\; c \in [0,\, 2^{64})
$$

where $k$ is the seed key and $c$ is the call counter.  After each
draw of a 128-bit output block, $c$ is incremented by 1.  The next
sample is always $\text{Philox}(k, c)$, so saving $(k, c)$ is a
lossless checkpoint of the generator.

returns.description:
1-D `int64` tensor `[seed, counter]` of shape `(2,)`.
Pass this directly to `set_rng_state` to restore the stream.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.manual_seed(0)
>>> _ = lucid.rand(10)           # advance counter by drawing 10 values
>>> state = lucid.get_rng_state()
>>> a = lucid.rand(5)
>>> lucid.set_rng_state(state)   # rewind
>>> b = lucid.rand(5)
>>> (a - b).abs().max().item()
0.0
notes:
Unlike Mersenne Twister (which requires 624 × 32-bit words of state),
Philox's full state is just 128 bits.  This makes checkpointing
essentially free and enables **exact reproducibility** of training
runs when saved alongside model weights.

members.name: set_rng_state
members.signature: set_rng_state(new_state: Tensor)
members.summary: Restore the default random generator to a previously captured state.
members.extended:
Rewinds (or fast-forwards) the Philox generator to the exact
`(seed, counter)` pair encoded in `new_state`, so that the next
sample call produces exactly the same value as it did immediately
after the `get_rng_state` call that created `new_state`.

Formally, after `set_rng_state(state)` the generator satisfies:

$$
k \leftarrow \texttt{state}[0], \quad
c \leftarrow \texttt{state}[1]
$$

and the next draw returns $\text{Philox}(k, c)$.

parameters.name: new_state
parameters.description:
Length-2 `int64` tensor `[seed, counter]` as returned by
`get_rng_state`.  Passing a tensor of any other shape or dtype
raises `ValueError`.

raises.description: If `new_state` does not have exactly 2 elements.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.manual_seed(99)
>>> state = lucid.get_rng_state()
>>> x = lucid.randn(4)
>>> lucid.set_rng_state(state)
>>> y = lucid.randn(4)
>>> (x - y).abs().max().item()
0.0

members.name: rand
members.signature: rand(size: _int | tuple[_int, ...] = (), dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False, generator: _C_engine.Generator | None = None)
members.summary: Return a tensor of samples drawn from the continuous uniform distribution.
members.extended:
Each element is drawn independently from $U[0, 1)$, the uniform
distribution on the half-open unit interval:

$$
X_i \sim U[0, 1), \quad
f_X(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & 0 \le x < 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
$$

The distribution has mean $\mathbb{E}[X] = \tfrac{1}{2}$ and variance
$\operatorname{Var}[X] = \tfrac{1}{12}$.

parameters.name: *size
parameters.description:
Shape of the output tensor.  Accepts varargs `rand(2, 3)` or a
single tuple `rand((2, 3))`.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description:
Floating-point data type.  Defaults to the global default
(`lucid.float32`).  Integer dtypes are not supported.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Target device — `"cpu"` or `"metal"`.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description:
If `True`, downstream operations are tracked by autograd.
Default: `False`.

parameters.name: generator
parameters.description:
Explicit generator to use.  When `None` (default), the global
default generator is used.

returns.description: Tensor of shape `size` with values in $[0, 1)$.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.manual_seed(0)
>>> x = lucid.rand(3, 4)
>>> x.shape
(3, 4)
>>> float(x.min()) >= 0.0 and float(x.max()) < 1.0
True
Monte-Carlo estimate of $\pi$:
>>> lucid.manual_seed(0)
>>> n = 1_000_000
>>> pts = lucid.rand(n, 2)
>>> inside = ((pts ** 2).sum(dim=-1) < 1.0).float().mean()
>>> abs(float(inside) * 4 - 3.1416) < 0.01
True

members.name: randn
members.signature: randn(size: _int | tuple[_int, ...] = (), dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False, generator: _C_engine.Generator | None = None)
members.summary: Return a tensor of samples drawn from the standard normal distribution.
members.extended:
Each element is drawn independently from $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, the
standard Gaussian with zero mean and unit variance:

$$
X_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1), \quad
f_X(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\, e^{-x^2 / 2}
$$

The distribution has mean $\mathbb{E}[X] = 0$, variance
$\operatorname{Var}[X] = 1$, and all odd central moments zero.

parameters.name: *size
parameters.description: Shape of the output tensor.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description: Floating-point data type.  Defaults to the global default.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Target device — `"cpu"` or `"metal"`.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description: Enable autograd tracking.  Default: `False`.

parameters.name: generator
parameters.description: Explicit generator.  Defaults to the global default generator.

returns.description: Tensor of shape `size` with $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ samples.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.manual_seed(0)
>>> x = lucid.randn(1000)
>>> abs(float(x.mean())) < 0.1       # ≈ 0
True
>>> abs(float(x.std()) - 1.0) < 0.1  # ≈ 1
True
Kaiming initialisation for a linear layer:
>>> fan_in = 256
>>> w = lucid.randn(fan_in, 512) * (2.0 / fan_in) ** 0.5
notes:
The engine uses the **Box–Muller transform** to convert pairs of
uniform samples $(u_1, u_2) \sim U(0,1)^2$ into standard normals:



$$
z_1 = \sqrt{-2\ln u_1}\,\cos(2\pi u_2), \quad
z_2 = \sqrt{-2\ln u_1}\,\sin(2\pi u_2)
$$

This is exact (not approximate) and is highly efficient on SIMD
hardware because the two outputs $z_1, z_2$ can be produced
simultaneously from one pair of uniform draws.

**Xavier / Glorot initialisation** (Glorot & Bengio, 2010) uses
$\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ with



$$
\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{2}{n_\text{in} + n_\text{out}}}
$$

which can be obtained as `randn(fan_in, fan_out) * sigma`.

**[He / Kaiming initialisation** (He et al., 2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.01852) for ReLU networks
uses $\sigma = \sqrt{2 / n_\text{in}}$.

members.name: randint
members.signature: randint(low: _int, high: _int, size: list[_int] | tuple[_int, ...], dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False, generator: _C_engine.Generator | None = None)
members.summary: Return a tensor of samples drawn from the discrete uniform distribution.
members.extended:
Each element is drawn independently and uniformly from the integer set
$\{l, l+1, \ldots, h-1\}$, i.e. the discrete uniform distribution:

$$
X_i \sim \mathcal{U}\{l,\, h-1\}, \quad
P(X_i = k) = \frac{1}{h - l}
\quad \forall\; k \in \{l, \ldots, h-1\}
$$

The distribution has mean $\mathbb{E}[X] = \tfrac{l + h - 1}{2}$ and
variance $\operatorname{Var}[X] = \tfrac{(h-l)^2 - 1}{12}$.

parameters.name: low
parameters.description: Lower bound of the interval (inclusive).

parameters.name: high
parameters.description:
Upper bound of the interval (exclusive).  Must satisfy
`high > low`.

parameters.name: size
parameters.description:
Shape of the output tensor.  Unlike `rand` / `randn`, `size`
is a single required keyword-positional argument, not varargs.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description: Integer data type.  Defaults to `lucid.int64`.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Target device — `"cpu"` or `"metal"`.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description:
Enable autograd tracking.  Default: `False`.  Gradients through
integer tensors are always zero; this flag is accepted for
compatibility with downstream wrappers.

parameters.name: generator
parameters.description: Explicit generator.  Defaults to the global default generator.

returns.description: Integer tensor of shape `size` with values in $[l, h)$.

raises.description:
`high <= low`, or `dtype` cannot hold `low` or `high - 1`
(`int8` past 127): such a draw used to wrap round.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.manual_seed(0)
>>> x = lucid.randint(0, 10, (5,))
>>> x.shape, x.dtype
((5,), lucid.int64)
>>> bool(((x >= 0) & (x < 10)).all())
True
>>> idx = lucid.randint(0, 1024, (64,))  # sample 64 indices
>>> mask = lucid.randint(0, 2, (3, 4))  # values in {0, 1}
notes:
The engine generates the integers via
$X_i = l + \lfloor U_i \cdot (h - l) \rfloor$ for $U_i \sim U[0, 1)$,
giving an exact discrete uniform distribution with no
acceptance–rejection overhead.  Common uses include sampling mini-batch
indices, generating random class labels, and stochastic depth masks.

members.name: bernoulli
members.signature: bernoulli(input: Tensor, p: _float | None = None, generator: _C_engine.Generator | None = None)
members.summary: Draw binary random numbers (`0` or `1`) from a Bernoulli distribution.
members.extended:
The `input` tensor holds probabilities in $[0, 1]$ to be used for
drawing the binary random number, unless scalar `p` is supplied, in which
case `input` provides only the output shape, dtype, and device while each
element is drawn from $\text{Bernoulli}(p)$.

$$
\text{out}_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_i), \quad
P(\text{out}_i = 1) = p_i, \quad P(\text{out}_i = 0) = 1 - p_i
$$

parameters.name: input
parameters.description:
Probability values for the Bernoulli distribution when `p` is `None`,
or shape/dtype/device template when `p` is given.

parameters.name: p
parameters.description:
If provided, uniform success probability in $[0, 1]$ used for all
elements.

parameters.name: generator
parameters.description: Explicit generator. Defaults to the global default.

returns.description:
Tensor of the same shape, dtype, and device as `input` with values in
$\{0, 1\}$.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.manual_seed(0)
>>> probs = lucid.full((10_000,), 0.3)
>>> x = lucid.bernoulli(probs)
>>> sorted(set(x.tolist()))                      # only zeros and ones
[0.0, 1.0]
>>> abs(float(x.mean()) - 0.3) < 0.02            # ≈ 30 % ones
True

members.name: normal
members.signature: normal(mean: _float = 0.0, std: _float = 1.0, size: list[_int] | tuple[_int, ...], dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False, generator: _C_engine.Generator | None = None)
members.summary: Return a tensor of samples drawn from a parametric normal distribution.
members.extended:
Each element is drawn independently from $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$:

$$
X_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\, \sigma^2), \quad
f_X(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,
         \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)
$$

with mean $\mathbb{E}[X_i] = \mu$ and standard deviation
$\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[X_i]} = \sigma$.

parameters.name: mean
parameters.description: Mean $\mu$ of the distribution.  Default: `0.0`.

parameters.name: std
parameters.description: Standard deviation $\sigma > 0$.  Default: `1.0`.

parameters.name: size
parameters.description: Shape of the output tensor.  Required (keyword-only).

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description: Floating-point data type.  Defaults to the global default.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Target device — `"cpu"` or `"metal"`.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description: Enable autograd tracking.  Default: `False`.

parameters.name: generator
parameters.description: Explicit generator.  Defaults to the global default.

returns.description: Tensor of shape `size` with $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ samples.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.manual_seed(0)
>>> x = lucid.normal(mean=5.0, std=2.0, size=(1000,))
>>> abs(float(x.mean()) - 5.0) < 0.2
True
>>> abs(float(x.std()) - 2.0) < 0.2
True
He-normal initialisation for a Conv2d kernel:
>>> fan_in = 3 * 3 * 64          # kernel_h × kernel_w × C_in
>>> w = lucid.normal(0.0, (2.0 / fan_in) ** 0.5, size=(128, 64, 3, 3))
notes:
This is a convenience wrapper around `randn` with an affine shift:



$$
X = \mu + \sigma \cdot Z, \quad Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)
$$

The output is therefore equivalent to
`mean + std * lucid.randn(*size, ...)`.

**Weight initialisation** recipes commonly parameterise the normal
distribution directly:

* **LeCun normal** (LeCun et al., 1998):
  $\sigma = \sqrt{1 / n_\text{in}}$
* **Glorot normal** (Glorot & Bengio, 2010):
  $\sigma = \sqrt{2 / (n_\text{in} + n_\text{out})}$
* **[He normal** (He et al., 2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.01852):
  $\sigma = \sqrt{2 / n_\text{in}}$

members.name: rand_like
members.signature: rand_like(input: Tensor, generator: _C_engine.Generator | None = None, dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False)
members.summary: Return a $U[0,1)$ random tensor with the same shape, dtype, and device as `input`.
members.extended:
Equivalent to `lucid.rand(t.shape, dtype=t.dtype, device=t.device)`,
but infers metadata from an existing tensor so the caller need not
repeat shape and type information.

Each element is drawn independently from

$$
X_i \sim U[0, 1)
$$

parameters.name: input
parameters.description:
Reference tensor.  Its `shape`, `dtype`, and `device` are
inherited by the output unless overridden.

parameters.name: generator
parameters.description:
Explicit generator.  Defaults to the default stream that
`manual_seed` controls — the one `rand` reads.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description: Override the data type.  Defaults to `t.dtype`.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Override the device.  Defaults to `t.device`.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description: Enable autograd tracking.  Default: `False`.

returns.description: Uniform random tensor shaped like `input`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> x = lucid.zeros(3, 4, device="metal")
>>> noise = lucid.rand_like(x)
>>> noise.shape, noise.device
((3, 4), device('metal'))
notes:
The returned tensor mirrors `input`'s `shape`, `dtype`, and
`device` exactly unless overridden via the corresponding keyword
arguments.  Sampling follows the same dtype-default rule as
`lucid.rand`: only floating-point dtypes are supported.  Calling
this on an integer tensor without overriding `dtype` raises — use
`lucid.randint` with an explicit shape for integer noise.

members.name: randn_like
members.signature: randn_like(input: Tensor, generator: _C_engine.Generator | None = None, dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False)
members.summary: Return a $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ random tensor with the same shape, dtype, and device as `input`.
members.extended:
Equivalent to `lucid.randn(t.shape, dtype=t.dtype, device=t.device)`,
inferring all metadata from an existing tensor.

Each element is drawn independently from the standard normal:

$$
X_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1), \quad
f_X(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-x^2/2}
$$

parameters.name: input
parameters.description:
Reference tensor whose `shape`, `dtype`, and `device` are
inherited unless overridden.

parameters.name: generator
parameters.description:
Explicit generator.  Defaults to the default stream that
`manual_seed` controls — the one `randn` reads.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description: Override the data type.  Defaults to `t.dtype`.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Override the device.  Defaults to `t.device`.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description: Enable autograd tracking.  Default: `False`.

returns.description: Standard-normal random tensor shaped like `input`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> w = lucid.zeros(256, 512, dtype=lucid.float16, device="metal")
>>> noise = lucid.randn_like(w)
>>> noise.shape, noise.dtype, noise.device
((256, 512), lucid.float16, device('metal'))
notes:
A common pattern in **noise injection** regularisation is to add
scaled Gaussian noise to activations or weights during training:



$$
\tilde{x} = x + \epsilon \cdot \mathcal{N}(0, I),
\quad \epsilon \ll 1
$$

`randn_like` makes this concise and device-safe:



```python
x_noisy = x + noise_scale * lucid.randn_like(x)
```

members.name: randint_like
members.signature: randint_like(input: Tensor, low: _int = 0, high: _int | None = None, generator: _C_engine.Generator | None = None, dtype: DTypeLike = None, device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False)
members.summary: Return random integers in $[\text{low}, \text{high})$ shaped like `input`.
members.extended:
Each element is drawn independently and uniformly from
$\{l, l+1, \ldots, h-1\}$, as `randint` draws them, in `input`'s
shape, dtype and device unless overridden.  Called with one bound by
position, `randint_like(x, 10)`, the bound is `high` and `low` is
`0`; `low=` alone is refused, as by the reference.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description:
Reference tensor whose `shape`, `dtype` and `device` the
result takes.

parameters.name: low
parameters.description: Lowest integer drawn (inclusive).  Default `0`.

parameters.name: high
parameters.description: One above the highest integer drawn (exclusive); required.

parameters.name: generator
parameters.description:
Explicit generator.  Defaults to the default stream that
`manual_seed` controls — the one `randint` reads.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description:
Override the data type.  Defaults to `input.dtype`: a floating
`input` gets floating values that are whole numbers.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Override the device.  Defaults to `input.device`.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description: Enable autograd tracking — floating dtypes only.  Default `False`.

returns.description:
Tensor of `input`'s shape with whole-number values in
$[\text{low}, \text{high})$.

raises.description:
A bound is not an integer, `high` is not given, or `low=` is
given without `high=`.

`low >= high`, or the result's dtype cannot hold `low` or
`high - 1` — `int8` past 127, bool past 1, a floating dtype past
its largest finite value (a `RuntimeError` and a `ValueError`).

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.manual_seed(0)
>>> x = lucid.zeros(2, 3)
>>> r = lucid.randint_like(x, 10)
>>> r.shape, r.dtype
((2, 3), lucid.float32)
>>> bool(((r >= 0) & (r < 10)).all())
True
>>> lucid.randint_like(x, 3, 4, dtype=lucid.int64).tolist()
[[3, 3, 3], [3, 3, 3]]
notes:
The integers are drawn as `int64` and cast to the result's dtype, so
the draw is the same on either device whatever that dtype is.

members.name: randperm
members.signature: randperm(n: _int, generator: _C_engine.Generator | None = None, dtype: DTypeLike = ..., device: DeviceLike = None, requires_grad: _bool = False)
members.summary: Return a uniformly random permutation of the integers $0, 1, \ldots, n-1$.
members.extended:
Produces a rank-1 tensor containing a uniformly random element of
$S_n$, the symmetric group of permutations on $n$ symbols.  Every
one of the $n!$ orderings is equally likely:

$$
P(\sigma) = \frac{1}{n!}
\quad \forall\; \sigma \in S_n
$$

parameters.name: n
parameters.description:
Number of elements.  Must be $\geq 0$.  Returns an empty tensor
when `n = 0`.

parameters.name: generator
parameters.description: Explicit generator.  Defaults to the global default.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description: Integer data type of the output.  Defaults to `lucid.int64`.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Target device — `"cpu"` or `"metal"`.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description: Enable autograd tracking.  Default: `False`.

returns.description:
1-D integer tensor of shape `(n,)` containing a permutation of
$\{0, 1, \ldots, n-1\}$.

raises.description: `n` is negative, or past what `dtype` holds exactly (int8: 128).

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.manual_seed(0)
>>> sorted(lucid.randperm(5).tolist())   # every index exactly once
[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
Shuffle a dataset of 1024 examples in one line:
>>> data = lucid.randn(1024, 16)
>>> idx = lucid.randperm(1024)
>>> shuffled = data[idx]
>>> shuffled.shape
(1024, 16)
Edge cases:
>>> lucid.randperm(0).shape
(0,)
>>> lucid.randperm(1).tolist()
[0]
notes:
The implementation uses the **lottery-ticket argsort trick**: assign
each integer $k$ a uniform random key $u_k \sim U[0,1)$ and return
the argsort of those keys:



$$
\pi = \operatorname{argsort}(u), \quad u_k \sim U[0,1)^n
$$

This is equivalent to the Fisher–Yates shuffle in expectation and
is more cache-friendly on SIMD hardware because the sort can be
vectorised without branch-dependent swaps.
